content: This review is one of six that evaluates primary medical treatment options for chronic rhinosinusitis. Chronic rhinosinusitis is a prevalent condition characterized by inflammation of the nasal and paranasal sinus linings, leading to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, facial pain or pressure, and anosmia. It can occur with or without nasal polyps. Intranasal corticosteroids are widely recommended for treatment due to the belief that inflammation plays a central role in the disease. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of intranasal corticosteroids in individuals with chronic rhinosinusitis. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, with the last search performed on August 11, 2015. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a minimum follow-up of three months, comparing intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., beclomethasone dipropionate, triamcinolone acetonide, flunisolide, budesonide) to placebo or no treatment in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis. Eighteen RCTs involving 2738 participants were included in the analysis. Fourteen studies focused on patients with nasal polyps, while four included those without polyps. Only one study involved children. The primary outcomes assessed were disease-specific health-related quality of life (HRQL), patient-reported disease severity, and the most common adverse event, epistaxis. Secondary outcomes included general HRQL, endoscopic nasal polyp scores, CT scan scores, and adverse events such as local irritation or systemic side effects. For disease-specific HRQL, only one study (20 adult participants without polyps) used the Rhinosinusitis Outcome Measures-31 (RSOM-31) and found no significant difference between intranasal corticosteroids and placebo (data not available, very low-quality evidence). Disease severity was assessed in another study (134 participants without polyps) using the Chronic Sinusitis Survey, which also found no meaningful difference (mean difference [MD] 2.84, 95% confidence interval [CI] -5.02 to 10.70; scale 0 to 100). However, a study involving patients with nasal polyps reported a higher likelihood of improvement in the corticosteroid group (risk ratio [RR] 2.78, 95% CI 1.76 to 4.40; 109 participants, low-quality evidence). Six studies provided data on at least two of the individual symptoms defined by the EPOS 2012 criteria (nasal blockage, rhinorrhea, anosmia, and facial pain/pressure). When all four symptoms were assessed on a 0 to 3 severity scale, the average MD in symptom change from baseline was -0.26 (95% CI -0.37 to -0.15; 243 participants; two studies; low-quality evidence). For nasal blockage and rhinorrhea alone, the MD was -0.31 (95% CI -0.38 to -0.24; 1702 participants; six studies). When anosmia was included, the MD was similar (-0.31; 1345 participants; four studies; moderate-quality evidence). Intranasal corticosteroids showed the greatest benefit for nasal blockage (MD -0.40, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.29; 1702 participants; six studies), followed by smaller benefits for rhinorrhea (MD -0.25, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.17; 1702 participants; six studies) and anosmia (MD -0.19, 95% CI -0.28 to -0.11; 1345 participants; four studies). There was variability in the results for facial pain/pressure (MD -0.27, 95% CI -0.56 to 0.02; 243 participants; two studies). The evidence quality was moderate for nasal blockage, rhinorrhea, and anosmia, but low for facial pain/pressure. The risk of epistaxis was significantly increased with intranasal corticosteroids (RR 2.74, 95% CI 1.88 to 4.00; 2508 participants; 13 studies; high-quality evidence). However, the severity of epistaxis was not consistently reported, and minor streaks of blood may not be clinically significant for patients. For general HRQL, one study (134 participants without polyps) used the SF-36 and found a statistically significant benefit only on the general health subscale (very low-quality evidence). The risk of local irritation was unclear (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.64; 2124 participants; 11 studies; low-quality evidence). None of the studies provided sufficient data on long-term risks such as osteoporosis or growth suppression in children. In conclusion, most of the evidence pertains to patients with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. There is limited information on quality of life (very low-quality evidence). Intranasal corticosteroids appear to improve disease severity for all symptoms (low-quality evidence), with moderate benefits for nasal blockage and smaller benefits for rhinorrhea (moderate-quality evidence). The risk of epistaxis is increased (high-quality evidence), but the clinical significance of minor bleeding is uncertain. The risk of local irritation remains unclear (low-quality evidence).
